query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles with enhanced surface passivation will exhibit reduced surface atomic diffusion, thereby suppressing phase segregation and preserving their metastable, single-phase solid solution structure under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions compared to identical nanoparticles without enhanced passivation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by physical or chemical routes in a well-mixed, metastable single-phase state.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled surface passivation treatment (via ligand exchange or thermal treatment) to reduce surface defect density without altering the bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature environments typical of catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications, under inert or controlled atmospheres to limit extraneous oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface defect density and the integrity of the passivation layer, which mediate the rate of surface and near-surface atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced surface passivation retards the diffusional mobility of atoms at the nanoparticle boundaries. This reduced mobility limits the thermodynamically driven phase segregation and elemental precipitation processes that would otherwise destabilize the metastable solid solution under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature conditions, passivated nanoparticles will show significantly less evidence of phase segregation (as observed via techniques such as X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy) compared to non-passivated controls. This should manifest as more uniform elemental distribution, less grain coarsening, and preservation of the single-phase structure.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with the same composition and microstructural properties but without any deliberate surface passivation treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to multi-element, low noble-metal content nanoparticles where surface diffusion is a dominant factor in high-temperature phase stability. It may not hold if additional environmental factors (e.g., aggressive oxidation conditions) overwhelm the benefits of surface passivation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the reduction in atomic diffusion and stabilization effect is uncertain and may depend on the type and quality of the passivation layer as well as on other processing variables. Additionally, interactions with high-temperature environments (e.g., oxidation kinetics) may complicate the isolation of the surface diffusion effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles. Treat one set with a surface passivation procedure (e.g., ligand exchange or controlled thermal treatment to reduce surface defects) and leave the other set untreated. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions within the catalytic (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes for a defined period. Characterize the structural evolution using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and elemental mapping before and after thermal treatment.
measurements: Nanostructure and grain boundary characteristics (via TEM)
Elemental distribution uniformity (via EDS or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant reduction in phase segregation, grain coarsening, or elemental inhomogeneity relative to the untreated nanoparticles under the same high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that surface passivation mitigates diffusion-driven instability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

decision.trend: Early studies on high‐entropy alloys have shown that achieving a metastable, single‐phase solid solution depends critically on the processing route – rapid quenching and careful control of composition can suppress phase precipitation and segregation. For example, PMC4999872 demonstrated that even small composition changes (e.g., in Al content) can tip the balance toward multiphase behavior under stress (here via irradiation), while PMC10384371 revealed that high‐temperature oxidation can trigger complex phase transformations and elemental segregation. Although these studies were not conducted on nanoparticles per se, they highlight that diffusion‐controlled processes (including surface and bulk atomic rearrangements) and oxidation are key players in stability. Over time, efforts have shifted from establishing phase stability in bulk or thin-film HEAs to identifying the kinetics of diffusion and precipitation, yet a systematic link between nanoparticle synthesis (with its inherently high surface‐to‐volume ratio and defect levels) and stability under high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric conditions remains unestablished.
decision.unsolved: Despite the insights gained from bulk and film studies, it remains unclear which kinetic factors – particularly those dominated by surface diffusion and related interfacial phenomena in nanoscale systems – govern whether metastable, near-equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles preserve their structure under high-temperature service conditions. The challenge is to isolate the role of surface (and near-surface) atomic mobility, including the influence of surface passivation or defect density, from the thermodynamic drive toward phase segregation and precipitation. Without this understanding, predicting and engineering stability for catalytic applications (with low noble-metal content) is still a major gap.
decision.lever: systematic variation of nanoparticle surface passivation (e.g., by ligand exchange or thermal treatments to modulate surface defect density)
decision.why: Because the trend in prior work demonstrates that stability under high-temperature conditions is linked to the kinetics of atomic diffusion and phase segregation, the most plausible next step is to conduct controlled experiments that vary only the nanoparticle surface chemistry. This lever isolates surface diffusion effects from bulk compositional factors, enabling a test of the hypothesis that enhanced surface passivation (thereby retarding diffusion at the particle boundaries) is critical to preserving the metastable solid solution. Comparing stability (via phase purity and resistance to segregation) of otherwise identical nanoparticles with different surface treatments will provide a clear, falsifiable test of whether surface-mediated diffusion is the dominant mechanism governing their service performance.
